tracks.title: The string that never runs
tracks.text: Lesson 03 point 7 — commands. A deep-dive, under the toolkit lesson. The toolkit page sold you a real program compiled to WebAssembly, then stopped at the unit. So here is the question that comes next. When an agent types jq, then grep, then upper… what actually runs? [curious] Is there a bash hiding under there? And what happens to the classic attack string — the one with a semicolon and remove-everything tacked onto the end? A command is a CLI converted to a sandboxed WASM module. Stdin in… stdout out… invoked by name through the Dock. It is the runnable half of a toolkit. The manual was the interface. The command is the muscle. And this lesson is mostly about one claim — that the oldest exploit in the book stops being something you defend against… and becomes something you can't even write down.

tracks.title: The string that runs
tracks.text: First — the string that runs. Every agent stack arrives at the same dirty moment. The model decides to run a tool… with a user's filename in it… and somewhere underneath, all of that gets glued into a single string and handed to a shell. The shell is the most powerful interpreter on the machine. And you just let a language model write programs for it… out of text it read on the internet. [sighs] The industry's answer has been the blocklist. Scan the string for a semicolon, for double-ampersand, for remove-dash-r-f, for backticks… and refuse the ones that look dangerous. But that's an apology, not a defense. A regular expression over a shell grammar is a regular expression over a grammar built to be re-quoted, encoded, and nested twelve ways. You're not winning that fight. You're announcing which round you lost. So this page asks a different question. Not how do we sanitize the command line… but what if the command line were never a string at all?

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A command is a CLI converted to a runnable WASM module — stdin in, stdout out — that a workbook or agent invokes by name… through the run-command Dock import. One name. One content-addressed artifact. One argument convention. A toolkit is the whole bundle — a progressive-disclosure skill doc bundled with the CLI it documents. The command is what that CLI becomes. Its runnable form. The manual tells an agent which commands exist… the commands are the verbs the manual is teaching. And a capability need — network, a directory, more memory — is not a separate layer underneath. It's a property of the command itself. Declared, and granted. Nothing more.

tracks.title: A PATH with no operating system
tracks.text: Next — a PATH with no operating system. There is no user-bin here, and no PATH variable to scan. There's a registry — an Elixir module — and looking up a name walks two layers. Picture it as one trip. A call comes in for jq. First it hits a dynamic map — everything agents and toolkits registered this session. Then the static built-ins are laid over the top, and merged last… so they always win the lookup. [curious] That merge order is a security decision, not an accident. The built-ins — upper, jq, grep, and wbox — are reserved, and unshadowable. A hostile registration cannot rebind jq to its own bytes. The trusted name resolves to the trusted artifact… always. And what it resolves to is a path into a content-addressed store, where the file is named by the hash of its own bytes. A few guardrails ring the registry. First, names must be plain — letters, digits, dot, dash, underscore. Second, the dynamic map is capped at four thousand and ninety-six entries, so a flood can't exhaust memory. Third, every registered path must canonicalize strictly inside that one store directory — point it anywhere else and it's refused before it can run. And here's the living part. Names hot-swap. Re-register a name and the binding is replaced in place — no restart. Calls already in flight finish on the old bytes… the next call sees the new ones. The registry is edited while it runs.

tracks.title: What one invocation costs
tracks.text: [curious] So what does one invocation actually cost? Not a function call into a shared process. A fresh wasmtime subprocess — born for this one run, and gone after it. And it runs inside a fixed, small envelope. Let me give you the limits, one at a time. First… a wall clock. Thirty seconds, then it's trapped — a hang is not forever. Second… fuel. Five billion instructions, so a tight loop that never blocks still burns out and traps. Third… a stdin cap of sixty-four megabytes — an oversized pipe is a clear error, not an out-of-memory crash. Fourth… an argv cap of two hundred and fifty-six kilobytes. That one used to blow the argument limit and fail silently. Now it's a stated error. And fifth… file access only to preopened directories — no path resolves outside what was explicitly handed in. The verdict across all five — a command can fail, loop, or overflow, and every one of those is a bounded, named outcome… instead of a way out. One more thing worth saying. A non-zero exit is usually just the guest's normal failure — grep found nothing, jq hit a parse error. So the output returns verbatim, and the status is preserved… which is exactly what lets a downstream double-ampersand or double-pipe make sense.

tracks.title: The six no's
tracks.text: Now — the six no's. Between an agent saying run-command and any wasm starting… stands the exec broker. And its first principle is the one most stacks skip — there is no real operating-system exec here. Only registered wasm commands run. Every request walks a deny ladder, in one exact order, and every denial is audited. Picture the guest handing a request to the broker, and the broker checking six gates in sequence. First gate — is this tenant revoked? If so, stop. Second — over quota? The rate limiter's floor is two thousand broker calls per second, per tenant. Past that, denied. Third — is allow set to false? It is, by default. Default-deny. Fourth — is the chain deeper than eight levels? Too deep, denied. Fifth — is the name in this Instance's allowlist? A name outside it is not granted. And sixth, last of all… is the name even registered? If nobody ever registered it… unknown command. [excited] Six refusals before bytes execute. Each one logged. And underneath all six, one design choice — exec is its own capability. Separate from commands, from storage, from networking. A profile can grant durable storage or the network… without ever granting the power to spawn a command. Because when exec isn't granted, its import isn't even merged into the guest. An un-granted capability isn't un-allowed. It's un-importable. Which makes it un-callable.

tracks.title: argv is a list, not a sentence
tracks.text: Here's the depth rung — argv is a list, not a sentence. And this is the whole trick. When an agent runs grep with the argument ada-semicolon-remove-everything… the broker never builds a string. It writes a length-prefixed structure, little-endian, and lays it out field by field. First, a length, then the name — g, r, e, p. Then a count — one argument. Then that argument's length… and then the bytes of the argument itself, including the semicolon — which is just byte three-B now, not syntax. Then the length of stdin, and the file bytes. [curious] There is no shell to interpret that semicolon. It crosses the boundary as the bytes of one discrete argument. Wasmtime receives a clean list of exactly two elements — grep, and the literal needle. And the most hostile thing that string can accomplish… is to not appear in the file. The classic injection class isn't mitigated here. It's unrepresentable. There's no field in this structure where a metacharacter could mean anything but itself. No delimiter… so no delimiter ambiguity. Two argument conventions ride this same wire. Most commands use real argv — the universal CLI interface. A couple of legacy interpreters, jq and grep, fold their filter or pattern into the first line of stdin instead. Either way… the argument never becomes shell text.

tracks.title: The shell that isn't one
tracks.text: Next — the shell that isn't one. Agents still want to type jq, pipe to grep, pipe to upper… and have it work. They can — and there is still no shell. The Workbooks shell is an Elixir pipeline evaluator. It parses the line, runs each stage as a registered WASM command, and pipes stdout into the next stage's stdin… in memory. No OS process. No fork. Just wasmtime per stage. Walk one pipeline, because it proves the whole thing. The line is jq quote dot-users-name quote, pipe, grep ada, pipe, upper. The shell splits it quote-aware — so jq's inner pipe, inside its quoted filter, stays inside its stage and never reads as a pipe. Stage one is jq, in stdin-first mode, so the filter becomes the first line of stdin ahead of the JSON. Fresh wasmtime — fuel five billion, thirty-second clock. Its stdout pipes on byte-exact, trailing newlines untouched… because trimming a newline here would make a downstream word-count lie. Stage two — grep, pattern on line one. Stage three — upper, argless, raw stdin. Three wasmtime processes. Zero shell forks. And the exit status of the last stage drives any double-ampersand that follows. The shell speaks a deliberate subset. Semicolon, double-ampersand, double-pipe, with real short-circuiting. Variables, with expansion — and an unknown name is left literal, so jq's own dollar-var survives. Redirection, confined to preopened directories — a path outside the sandbox is a clean error. And two tokens are intentional no-ops — redirecting standard-error to dev-null, and merging it into standard-out, are swallowed silently. Choking on those was once the single biggest source of per-run thrash. wbox, one binary compiled from C, supplies the everyday verbs as applets — cat, echo, head, word-count, sort, uniq, and a dozen more. Bash ergonomics… zero forks.

tracks.title: Sixty-some programs, each a row of data
tracks.text: Now — sixty-some programs, each a row of data. None of this would matter if the command set were a toy. It isn't. Around sixty-four real programs are seeded and live, each one proved by actually running it under wasmtime. And each one is, fundamentally, just data — a name, a URL, a sha-two-fifty-six pin, a wasm path, an arg mode. There are three lanes. First… the prebuilt fetch lane. Its trust gate is a single hash pin — the bytes are inert until run. This lane brings CPython three-twelve, Ruby, PHP, pandoc, OpenSSL, SQLite, Prolog… and the whole WebAssembly binary toolkit, which fans out from one tarball into twelve separate commands. Second… the C-source lane. Its gate is a pinned tarball, compiled in-sandbox by a wasm clang. This brings Lua, Z-standard, libsodium, P-C-R-E-two, and around twenty-seven names in all. Third… the inline lane. Its gate is the Instance's own profile caps — and this is where agents write their own, in Rust, Python, or JavaScript. The verdict across the three — trust scales with origin, not with effort. A prebuilt is trusted exactly as far as its hash. A C tool, as far as its pinned tarball. An inline command, only as far as the profile that built it. Here's one real row, read aloud. Name… python. Kind… wasm. A URL to the CPython three-twelve release. A sha that begins e-five-d-c. And mode… argv. CPython in the sandbox is four lines of data. And seeding happens at boot, inside a background task… so fetching the catalog never blocks the engine from starting.

tracks.title: Bytes that prove themselves
tracks.text: Another depth rung — bytes that prove themselves. A name resolving to bytes is only safe if the bytes can't lie. So every lane funnels through one content-addressing spine. Trace it. First… bytes arrive — fetched over a pure-Erlang T-L-S request that verifies against the operating system's trust store. There is no curl binary anywhere; a fetch is Erlang and T-L-S, full stop. Or the bytes are built in-sandbox by a wasm compiler. Second… they're hashed with sha-two-fifty-six, and that hash is the filename. Third… the same bytes always land on the same path, so registration is idempotent. Fourth… the name-to-path binding is written to a manifest, so a reboot re-registers everything with no re-fetch and no rebuild. And fifth — the closure that matters — at run time, the file is re-hashed, and refused on mismatch. That closes the gap between checking a file and using it, the gap a path-based store would leave wide open. The same posture extends outward. A workbook bundle carries its commands as wasm parts, and installing one never widens capabilities. A third-party toolkit with bad provenance refuses to build at all. And a toolkit whose binary name collides with a reserved name is rejected before it compiles — because the reserved set wins there too. The native escape hatches other stacks lean on — install-a-crate, fetch-a-go-package, native compilers — return explicit unavailable errors here, rather than shelling out. wasmtime running a wasm file is the architecture. Native binaries… are banned.

tracks.title: Commands that write commands
tracks.text: Next — commands that write commands. The catalog is not a fixed menu. Agents extend it, mid-session. With one CLI call — toolkit build-inline, a name, a language, a file — an agent writes source in Rust, C, Zig, JavaScript, or Go… and gets back a new registered command. And the astonishing part is what does the compiling. [excited] The compiler is itself wasm. Write… build… content-address… register — all inside the sandbox. No native toolchain. No host escape. Read the output of one run. The agent builds a word-frequency tool in Rust. The engine reports — built and registered command, w-freq, in Rust, written to the content-addressed store — run it via the Dock with run-command w-freq. And here's the safety. Self-authoring never widens caps. That new command holds exactly the capabilities its Instance profile granted — nothing more — because it was built by a process that itself held only those caps. The other direction up the ladder is promotion. An inline command that proves useful gets materialized into a real toolkit directory, where Org owns the spec and WASM owns the artifact. Promotion persists the source… not just the compiled bytes. Session, to workspace, to registry.

tracks.title: The honest edges
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where this construct stops. The shell is a subset, on purpose. No globbing. No subshells. No command substitution. And standard-error isn't real plumbing — redirecting it to dev-null is a swallowed no-op, not a redirection. If you need full POSIX shell theatre… this isn't it. If you need a safe way to chain wasm commands… it is. The banned native lanes are a choice, not a gap. Install-a-crate, fetch-a-go-package, and native compilers return an unavailable error rather than quietly shelling out to a real toolchain. We'd rather hand you an honest error than a hidden escape. The same honesty applies to depth. The broker's eight-level recursion bound is plumbed and tested — a depth-ninety-nine call returns a max-depth error in the suite. But an ordinary plain command has no exec import at all — only Dock-harness artifacts can nest. So we won't claim live deep command chains beyond what actually ships. The bound is real… the nesting it bounds is narrow today. And cold builds are slow — a C tool compiled by wasm clang the first time is not instant. But it's content-addressed, so it's a one-time cost. The second run is a hash lookup. And some software just fights the crossing — not everything native compiles cleanly to the WebAssembly system interface. When it doesn't… we say so.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Is this bash? No — and that's the entire point. No shell process, no command line. The shell is a pipeline evaluator, each stage a separate wasmtime subprocess, and arguments cross as a structural list. Why didn't my command see my file? Because a command can only reach preopened directories. If you didn't preopen the directory the file lives in, there's no path inside the sandbox that resolves to it. Grant the directory, and it appears. Can a hostile command hijack jq? No. The built-in names are reserved and merged last, so a registration can never shadow them — and a toolkit that even declares a colliding binary name is refused before it compiles. What if it infinite-loops? Two independent traps. A thirty-second wall clock, and a five-billion-instruction fuel budget — so a loop that never yields still runs out of fuel. Can I run my favorite CLI? Probably — in order of effort. A prebuilt build is four lines of data. C source builds in-sandbox. And if neither, write a small command yourself. [chuckles] What you can't do is shell out to a native binary. And last — what's the difference between the commands cap and the exec cap? Commands is the broad surface. Exec is a dedicated least-privilege cap that governs spawning. They're separate so a profile can store and fetch… without ever being able to run a command.

tracks.title: Back up to the toolkit
tracks.text: So that's commands. A CLI converted to sandboxed WASM — invoked by name, fed by stdin, answering on stdout. The runnable half of a toolkit, where the injection class isn't blocked… it's unrepresentable. Around sixty-four real programs, each just a row of data, and agents authoring more, in the sandbox, mid-session. [curious] If you want the layer this is the muscle of, the way back up is short. The parent is the toolkit lesson — lesson three — where the manual is the interface, and the command is what the manual teaches. Everything here is that bundle, seen from the side that runs.
